topics.title: Variables, types, and numbers
topics.why: Module 2 is entirely about counting: how many tokens does a piece of text cost. That's arithmetic on a variable, nothing more, but if you're not fluent with Python's basic types first, the arithmetic itself becomes the obstacle.

body.text: A variable is a name pointing at a value. Python figures out the type from the value itself, you don't declare it up front.

body.title: core types
body.text: `int` (whole numbers), `float` (decimals), `str` (text), `bool` (True/False). `len(x)` returns the length of a string, list, or dict. `//` is integer (floor) division, it drops any remainder, which matters when you're estimating a whole number of tokens.

body.code:
text = "Reset your password from Settings."
char_count = len(text)          # 35
approx_tokens = char_count // 4  # 8  (floor division, no remainder)
print(approx_tokens)

practice.question: Why floor division (`//`) instead of regular division (`/`) for a token estimate?
practice.answer: A token count has to be a whole number, you can't have "7.25 tokens." Regular division would give a float; floor division gives a clean integer, matching what a real token count actually is.

topics.title: Strings and basic pattern matching
topics.why: Module 1 opens with a real, common failure: a model wraps its JSON answer in a markdown code fence. Before you can parse that as JSON, you have to strip the fence off as a plain string operation.

body.text: Python strings support slicing, methods like `.strip()` and `.startswith()`, and the `re` module for pattern matching when a fixed check isn't enough.

body.title: regex for structural stripping
body.text: `re.match(pattern, text)` tests whether `text` starts with a match for `pattern` and gives you access to captured groups. `match.group(1)` returns whatever the first `(...)` in the pattern captured.

body.code:
import re

raw = '```json\n{"status": "ok"}\n```'
m = re.match(r"^```(?:json)?\s*([\s\S]*?)\s*```$", raw)
inner = m.group(1) if m else raw.strip()
print(inner)   # {"status": "ok"}

practice.question: What should your function do if the text ISN'T wrapped in a fence at all?
practice.answer: Return the text unchanged (just stripped of surrounding whitespace). A fence-stripping function shouldn't assume every input has a fence, plenty of valid model output won't.

topics.title: Lists and iteration
topics.why: Module 2's chunker splits a document into pieces that fit a token budget. Before tackling that token-aware version, get comfortable with the simpler idea underneath it: splitting a list into fixed-size groups.

body.text: A Python list is an ordered, mutable sequence. `list[start:end]` slices it; `.append(x)` adds to the end.

body.title: building a list of lists
body.text: A common pattern: start with an empty result list, loop over your input in fixed-size steps, and `.append()` each slice as its own sub-list.

body.code:
items = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
size = 2
batches = []
for i in range(0, len(items), size):
    batches.append(items[i:i + size])
print(batches)   # [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]

practice.question: What does `items[i:i+size]` return when `i+size` goes past the end of the list?
practice.answer: Python slicing never raises an out-of-range error, it just returns whatever is left, even if that's fewer than `size` items (or an empty list). This is why the last batch above has only 1 item, not a crash.

topics.title: Dictionaries
topics.why: Nearly everything an AI system configures, model parameters, tool schemas, retrieval settings, is a dict. A common pattern across every module ahead: start from sane defaults, then let a caller override just the parts they care about.

body.text: A dict maps keys to values. `{**a, **b}` builds a new dict by unpacking `a` first, then `b`, so `b`'s keys win on any overlap, without mutating either original dict.

body.title: non-destructive merging
body.text: Mutating a shared defaults dict in place is a common bug, the next caller gets a defaults dict that's no longer default. Building a NEW dict avoids that entirely.

practice.question: Why does `defaults` stay unchanged after building `config`?
practice.answer: `{**defaults, **overrides}` creates a brand-new dict, it reads from both inputs but writes to neither. Contrast with `defaults.update(overrides)`, which WOULD mutate `defaults` in place, a common source of bugs when the same defaults dict is reused across calls.

topics.title: Conditionals, loops, and sorting
topics.why: Module 3's whole job is retrieval: score every candidate, throw out the irrelevant ones, keep only the best few. That's a filter, a sort, and a slice, the exact combination this topic builds.

body.text: `sorted(iterable, key=..., reverse=True)` returns a new sorted list without changing the original. A list comprehension like `[x for x in items if condition]` filters in one line.

body.title: filter, sort, then limit, in that order
body.text: Filtering AFTER sorting (or slicing before filtering) can silently drop a result that should have made the cut. The safe order is always: score everything, filter out what doesn't qualify, sort what's left, then take only as many as you need.

body.code:
docs = [{"id": "a", "score": 0.9}, {"id": "b", "score": 0.2}, {"id": "c", "score": 0.6}]
qualified = [d for d in docs if d["score"] >= 0.4]
ranked = sorted(qualified, key=lambda d: d["score"], reverse=True)
top2 = ranked[:2]
print(top2)   # [{'id': 'a', 'score': 0.9}, {'id': 'c', 'score': 0.6}]

practice.question: Why filter by the minimum score BEFORE slicing to the limit, rather than after?
practice.answer: Slicing first (say, taking the top 2 by score, then checking if they clear the threshold) can leave you with fewer than you should have, or wrongly include a low scorer if you slice before sorting. Filtering first guarantees every candidate you keep already qualifies, however many end up in the final slice.

exercise.solution:
def top_matches(docs, min_score, limit):
    qualified = [d for d in docs if d["score"] >= min_score]
    ranked = sorted(qualified, key=lambda d: d["score"], reverse=True)
    return ranked[:limit]

topics.title: Functions and handling failure with try/except
topics.why: Module 7's eval harness has one hard rule: a single broken test case can never crash the whole evaluation run. That discipline starts here, with the basic shape of a function that fails safely instead of taking the whole program down with it.

body.text: A function that might fail should say so through its return value, not by letting an exception escape uncaught. `try/except` catches an error and lets you decide what happens next.

body.title: try/except
body.text: `try:` wraps code that might raise. `except Exception as e:` catches it, `e` is the exception object, `str(e)` gives its message. Code inside `except` runs only if the `try` block actually raised.

practice.question: What would happen to a caller looping over many `(a, b)` pairs if `safe_score` DIDN'T catch the exception?
practice.answer: A single `b=0` pair anywhere in the loop would raise, uncaught, and crash the ENTIRE loop, losing every result computed so far, not just the one bad pair. This is exactly the "one bad input shouldn't take down the whole batch" principle that shows up again in Module 4's tool executor and Module 7's eval harness.

topics.title: Working with JSON
topics.why: Every model API speaks JSON. Module 1's entire premise is that a model's JSON-shaped output can't be trusted until it's actually been parsed and validated, starting with just getting `json.loads()` to succeed.

body.text: Python's built-in `json` module converts between JSON text and Python objects. `json.loads(text)` parses text into a dict/list/etc; `json.dumps(obj)` does the reverse.

body.title: json.loads() raises on invalid input
body.text: Malformed JSON doesn't return `None`, it raises `json.JSONDecodeError`. If you want a function that never crashes on bad input, you have to catch that explicitly.

practice.question: Why is returning `None` on failure better than letting `json.JSONDecodeError` propagate out of your own function?
practice.answer: A caller expecting "either parsed data or a clear signal it failed" can check `if result is None` and handle it gracefully. An uncaught exception instead forces every single caller to wrap every single call in its own try/except, or risk a crash, exactly the repair-then-validate discipline Module 1 builds on.

topics.title: Async functions: the shape of a model API call
topics.why: Every real model API call is asynchronous, your code sends a request and waits for a response without freezing everything else. Module 6's entire retry-and-fallback system is built from `async def` functions and `await`. This is the minimum shape you need before that module.

body.text: `async def` defines a function that can be `await`ed. Inside an async function, `await some_async_call()` pauses until that call finishes, without blocking anything else.

body.title: trying calls in order until one works
body.text: A common async pattern (and the direct precursor to Module 6's fallback logic): try a list of async operations one at a time, and use the first one that succeeds, catching failures along the way instead of stopping at the first error.

practice.question: If EVERY call in the list raises, what should `fetch_first_success` return, and why not let the last exception propagate?
practice.answer: It should return `None` (a clear, structured "nothing worked" signal), not let an exception escape. This is the exact same "never let this function raise, report failure through the return value" discipline from topics 6 and 7, now applied to async code, and it's precisely what Module 6's `call_with_retry_fallback` builds on directly.
